cse-2017-2-cs-2.approach: Read each declaration or statement for what it does to memory: storage class, lost pointer, array of pointers, register hint.

steps.body: `static char var;` has static storage duration, so it lives in the data/BSS section, giving (ii). `register int var1;` asks the compiler to keep the variable in a CPU register, giving (iii).

cse-2017-2-cs-3.approach: Recall the standard running time of each algorithm, then match.

steps.title: Towers of Hanoi and binary search
steps.body: Hanoi: $T(n) = 2T(n-1)+1$, so $T(n) = 2^n - 1 = \Theta(2^n)$, giving (iii). Binary search halves the range each probe: $\Theta(\log n)$, giving (iv).

steps.title: Heap sort and matrix addition
steps.body: Heap sort: build-heap $O(n)$ plus $n$ delete-max operations at $O(\log n)$ each, so $\Theta(n\log n)$ in the worst case, giving (ii). Adding two $n\times n$ matrices touches $n^2$ entries once each: $\Theta(n^2)$, giving (i).

Swaps Hanoi and binary search, and also swaps heap sort and matrix addition.
Correct matching.

cse-2017-2-cs-4.approach: Use the CFL closure table: CFLs are closed under union and under intersection with a regular language, but not under complement or intersection.

steps.title: I and III hold
steps.body: I: union of two CFGs is a CFG ($S \to S_1 \mid S_2$). III: $L_1 - R = L_1 \cap \overline{R}$, and $\overline{R}$ is regular, so this is a CFL intersected with a regular language, which is context-free (product of a PDA with a DFA).

steps.title: II and IV fail in general
steps.body: IV: $\{a^nb^nc^m\} \cap \{a^mb^nc^n\} = \{a^nb^nc^n\}$, which is not context-free. II: if CFLs were closed under complement, then $L_1 \cap L_2 = \overline{\overline{L_1} \cup \overline{L_2}}$ would always be context-free, contradicting IV.

optionAnalysis.reason: Includes II and IV, and CFLs are not closed under complement or intersection.
Correct: only union and difference with a regular set are always context-free.
II and IV are exactly the two properties that fail.
Misses III; $L_1 - R = L_1 \cap \overline{R}$ is always context-free.

pitfalls: Thinking $L_1 - R$ needs closure under difference of CFLs; here $R$ is regular, so its complement is regular too.
cse-2017-2-cs-4.verification: The counterexample $\{a^nb^nc^n\}$ fails the pumping lemma for CFLs, confirming IV (and hence II) is false.

steps.title: Hierarchy
steps.body: Every SLR(1) grammar is LALR(1), and every LALR(1) grammar is LR(1), each inclusion proper: $\text{SLR} \subset \text{LALR} \subset \text{CLR}$.

steps.title: Per-thread items
steps.body: Each thread runs independently, so it has its own program counter, register set and stack (for its own call chain and local variables). I, II and IV are private.

cse-2017-2-cs-8.approach: External fragmentation arises only when a file needs one contiguous run of free blocks; schemes that can place blocks anywhere avoid it.

steps.title: Contiguous
steps.body: A file needs a run of consecutive free blocks, so free space breaks into holes that may be too small: external fragmentation. Not allowed.

steps.title: Linked and indexed
steps.body: Linked allocation chains blocks anywhere on disk, and indexed allocation lists arbitrary block numbers in an index block. Any free block can be used, so neither has external fragmentation. II and III qualify.

optionAnalysis.reason: Includes contiguous allocation, which suffers from external fragmentation.
Misses indexed allocation, which also uses any free block.
Misses linked allocation, which also uses any free block.
Correct: linked and indexed allocation both avoid external fragmentation.

cse-2017-2-cs-8.verification: Both linked and indexed schemes only waste space inside the last block (internal fragmentation) plus pointer/index overhead, never unusable gaps between files.

cse-2017-2-cs-10.approach: Use the derivative condition to get R and the integral condition to get S.

steps.title: Derivative condition gives R
steps.body: $f'(x) = \frac{R\pi}{2}\cos\frac{\pi x}{2}$. At $x=\frac12$: $\frac{R\pi}{2}\cos\frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{R\pi}{2}\cdot\frac{\sqrt2}{2} = \frac{R\pi\sqrt2}{4} = \sqrt2$, so $R = \frac{4}{\pi}$.

steps.title: Integral condition gives S
steps.body: $\int_0^1 R\sin\frac{\pi x}{2}\,dx = R\left[-\frac{2}{\pi}\cos\frac{\pi x}{2}\right]_0^1 = R\cdot\frac{2}{\pi}(1-0) = \frac{2R}{\pi}$, and $\int_0^1 S\,dx = S$. So $\frac{2R}{\pi} + S = \frac{2R}{\pi}$, giving $S = 0$.

$S = 0$ is right but $R = \frac{2}{\pi}$ gives $f'(\frac12) = \frac{\sqrt2}{2}$.
Correct: $R = \frac{4}{\pi}$, $S = 0$.
$R$ is right but $S = \frac{16}{\pi}$ would make the integral $\frac{2R}{\pi} + \frac{16}{\pi}$.

cse-2017-2-cs-13.approach: For O(1) enqueue at REAR and dequeue at FRONT, the only extra link needed is REAR→FRONT, which makes the list circular.

steps.title: Normal links
steps.body: Nodes link front to rear: FRONT → … → REAR. Dequeue moves FRONT to FRONT->next in O(1). Enqueue writes REAR->next = new node and moves REAR, also O(1).

steps.body: For the list to be circular, the rear node’s next pointer must point back to the front node (II). Statement I would make the front node point to the rear, which breaks the chain FRONT → second node, so dequeue could not find the new front in O(1).

cse-2017-2-cs-15.approach: In BFS, once a vertex is dequeued, all its unvisited neighbours are enqueued together and must be visited before any vertex discovered later. Test each order against this rule.
cse-2017-2-cs-15.given: Edges: M–N, N–O, M–R, M–Q, N–Q, O–Q, O–P, Q–P.

steps.title: Start at P
steps.body: Option D starts at P. Neighbours of P: O, Q. Enqueue them in the order O, Q. Visited: P.

steps.title: Dequeue O, then Q
steps.body: O’s unvisited neighbour is N, so the queue becomes [Q, N]. Q’s unvisited neighbour is M, so the queue becomes [N, M]. Visited so far: P, O, Q.

steps.title: Dequeue N, then M
steps.body: N adds nothing new. M adds R, which is then dequeued. The order P, O, Q, N, M, R matches option D.

scene.caption: Order: P O Q N M R

steps.title: Reject the others
steps.body: A: after M come its neighbours N, Q, R, but O comes third and O is not adjacent to M. B: after N come M, O, Q; P comes before O, yet P is not a neighbour of N. C: after Q come M, N, O, P; R comes fourth, before O and P.

optionAnalysis.reason: O is visited third, before M’s neighbours Q and R, but O is not adjacent to M.
P is visited before O, but P is not adjacent to N (P is only discovered from O or Q).
R is visited before O and P, but R is reached only through M, which is enqueued alongside O and P.
Correct: a valid BFS order from P.

pitfalls: Checking only adjacency of consecutive letters (that is a DFS-style check) instead of the layer-by-layer FIFO rule.
cse-2017-2-cs-15.verification: Layers from P: {P}, {O, Q}, {N, M}, {R}. D visits the layers in order, and the order within each layer matches the enqueue order.

cse-2017-2-cs-16.approach: Find what each variable generates and concatenate.

steps.title: X and Y
steps.body: $X \to aX \mid a$ generates $a^k$ with $k \ge 1$. $Y \to aYb \mid \epsilon$ generates $a^n b^n$ with $n \ge 0$.

cse-2017-2-cs-17.approach: R’s table can be folded into A’s table when each A entity is related to at most one B, that is, A is on the many side. Total participation of A means the merged foreign key column is never NULL.

steps.title: Cardinality
steps.body: If R is many-to-one from A to B, each A row relates to at most one B row, so B’s key can be stored as one column (foreign key) in A’s table. If R were one-to-many, an A entity could relate to many B’s and one column could not hold them all; the merge would have to go into B instead.

steps.title: Participation
steps.body: With total participation of A, every A row has a B partner, so the foreign key column has no NULLs and the merge is clean. This is the condition the question expects: many-to-one with total participation of A.

answer.value: Relationship R is many-to-one and the participation of A in R is total.

optionAnalysis.reason: One-to-many from A: an A entity may relate to several B’s, so R cannot be absorbed into A’s table.
Same cardinality problem as A.
Correct: A is on the many side, and total participation avoids NULL foreign keys.
The merge is possible in principle, but partial participation leaves NULL foreign keys for unrelated A rows; the standard (and expected) condition is total participation.

pitfalls: Reading “one-to-many” from B’s side; the relation is read from A to B as written.
cse-2017-2-cs-17.verification: This matches the textbook rule: for a 1:N relationship, put the key of the “1” side into the table of the “N” side, preferring the side with total participation.

cse-2017-2-cs-18.approach: A connected UDP socket fixes one default peer address; calling connect again just replaces (or clears) that address.

steps.title: Statement I
steps.body: After `connect`, the kernel records one peer address: `send` goes only to it and datagrams from any other address are discarded. So the socket cannot talk to multiple peers at the same time. I is false.

steps.title: Statement II
steps.body: Unlike TCP, a UDP socket may call `connect` again, either to set a new peer or (with family `AF_UNSPEC`) to disconnect. II is true.

optionAnalysis.reason: I is false: a connected UDP socket is bound to a single peer.
Correct.
I is false.
II is true: UDP connect can be repeated.

pitfalls: Applying TCP rules (connect may be called only once) to UDP.
cse-2017-2-cs-18.verification: This is standard Linux/BSD behaviour as documented in the connect(2) man page and in Stevens, UNP §8.11–8.12.

cse-2017-2-cs-19.approach: Follow the referential actions: deleting a T1 row triggers T2’s ON DELETE action on rows whose S references it; only a cascade into T2 could, in turn, cascade back to T1.

steps.title: Who references ⟨3, 8⟩?
steps.body: The row has $P = 3$. In T2, $S$ references $T1.P$; the only row with $S = 3$ is $\langle 8, 3\rangle$. Its rule is ON DELETE SET NULL, so it becomes $\langle 8, \text{NULL}\rangle$. It is not deleted.

steps.title: Any chain back to T1?
steps.body: T1 rows are deleted only when a referenced T2 row (via $Q \to R$, ON DELETE CASCADE) is deleted. No T2 row is deleted, so no further T1 row is deleted. Answer: **0**.

pitfalls: Assuming that deleting $\langle 3, 8\rangle$ cascades to T2 row $R = 8$ and then to T1 rows with $Q = 8$; the cascade direction is from the referenced table to the referencing table, and T2's action is SET NULL.
cse-2017-2-cs-19.verification: Q = 8 in T1 refers to R = 8 in T2; deleting the T1 row (a referencing row) never deletes the T2 row it points to.

cse-2017-2-cs-20.approach: IPv4 options take at most 40 bytes; the record route option spends 3 bytes on type, length and pointer, and each address takes 4 bytes.

steps.title: Space available
steps.body: Max header 60 bytes minus fixed 20 bytes leaves 40 bytes for options. RR overhead: type (1) + length (1) + pointer (1) = 3 bytes, leaving $40 - 3 = 37$ bytes.

steps.title: Number of addresses
steps.body: $\lfloor 37/4 \rfloor = 9$ addresses (using 36 bytes; 1 byte is left over).

cse-2017-2-cs-21.approach: Check whether every pair of elements already has a least upper bound and a greatest lower bound; if so, nothing needs to be added.

steps.title: Comparable pairs
steps.body: $a$ is below everything and $e$ is above everything, and $a \le b \le c \le e$, $a \le d \le e$. Any comparable pair $x \le y$ has lub $y$ and glb $x$.

steps.title: Incomparable pairs
steps.body: Incomparable pairs are $\{b, d\}$ and $\{c, d\}$. Upper bounds of $b$ and $d$: $\{e\}$, so lub $= e$; lower bounds: $\{a\}$, so glb $= a$. Upper bounds of $c$ and $d$: $\{e\}$, so lub $= e$; lower bounds: $\{a\}$, so glb $= a$.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: Every pair has a lub and a glb, so $(X, R)$ is already a lattice (the pentagon $N_5$). Pairs to add: **0**.

pitfalls: Confusing “lattice” with “distributive lattice”; $N_5$ is not distributive, but it is a lattice.
cse-2017-2-cs-21.verification: A finite poset with a top element in which every pair has a glb is a lattice; here $e$ is the top and every pair has glb $a$ or the smaller element.
